column2: The body belongs to earth; the essence to water; the eyes are said to belong to light; wind rests on the breaths; space is in the cavities of the embodied.
Vishnu is in the stride, Shakra in strength, fire in the belly digests what is eaten; the quarters are in the ears, and speech, Sarasvati, in the tongue.
Ears, skin, eyes, tongue and nose as fifth: the views spoken of the senses are doors for the accomplishment of food.
This is not seen by the eye nor by all the senses; the great self shines by a mind well kindled.
Without sound, touch or form, tasteless and scentless, imperishable, bodiless, senseless, it should be seen in one's own body.
He who sees the unmanifest in manifest bodies, the immortal resting in mortals, becomes after death fit for Brahman.
In a brahmana endowed with learning and birth, in a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater, the wise see alike.
He dwells in all beings, moving and fixed, the one great self by whom all this is pervaded.
When the self of beings sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, then he attains Brahman.
As great as the self is in the self, so great is the self in the supreme self; he who thus always knows becomes fit for immortality.
Even the gods are bewildered on the path of the one who is the self of all beings and ever for the good of all, seeking the footprint of the footless.
As the course of birds in the sky or of water creatures in water is not seen, so is that of the very great soul.
Time cooks all beings in the self by the self; but in whom Time is cooked, no one here knows.
It does not take hold above, sideways, below, across or in the middle, nor does anyone take it from anywhere.
All these worlds are within; nothing of them is outside; one who might meet a thousand, like an arrow fallen from its string,
would never reach the end of the cause, even if his speed were that of the mind; so there is nothing subtler than the subtle, nor grosser than that.
It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and faces everywhere, ears everywhere in the world; it stands covering all.
That is smaller than the atom, greater than the great; within all beings it stays firm and is not seen.
The imperishable and the perishable are this twofold state of the self; the perishable is in all beings; the divine immortal is imperishable.
Having gone to the city of nine gates, the swan, restrained and master, is lord of all beings, fixed and moving.
Through the abandonment and breaking of the new bodies' variations and their resort, those who see the far shore say the unborn is a swan.
What is spoken by the swan and the imperishable, the unchanging, that imperishable: knowing it, one gains the imperishable and gives up the breaths and birth.
[Vyasa said:] "I shall tell you all the duty of yoga; hear it. Oneness of intellect, mind and all the senses, for one meditating on the self, dear, this is the highest knowledge.
That is to be understood by one who is calm, self-controlled, devoted to the self, delighting in the self, awakened, of pure deeds.
Cutting off the five faults of yoga which the wise know: desire, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as fifth.
Anger is conquered by calm, desire by giving up intentions; the steadfast should cut off sleep by cultivating goodness.
By steadiness one should guard the organ and belly; the hands and feet by the eye; the eye and ear by the mind; the mind and speech by action.
By heedfulness he should give up fear, and greed by serving the wise; thus he should conquer these faults of yoga, ever untiring.
He should honour the fires and brahmanas, bow to the deities, and avoid angry speech joined with violence that follows the mind.
His semen is made of Brahma's energy, whose essence is all this; of the one being, being is twofold, moving and unmoving.
Meditation, study, giving, truth, modesty, honesty, forbearance, purity, purity of food, and restraint of the senses:
by these energy grows and sin is drawn off; all his aims are accomplished and discernment goes on.

Equal to all beings, living on what comes or does not come, with sin shaken off, full of energy, light of diet, master of senses, having brought desire and anger under control, he should wish to lead himself to the seat of Brahman.
Having made the mind and senses one-pointed, collected, he should hold the mind by the self in the early and late hours of the night.
Of this five-sensed creature, if one sense is a hole, from it wisdom leaks away, as water from a leather bag at the foot.
He should first seize the mind, as a fisherman small fish; then the ear, the eye, the tongue and the nose, the knower of yoga.
Having restrained these, the ascetic should set them in the mind; likewise, removing intentions, he should hold the mind in the self.
Having joined the five with knowledge, the ascetic should set them in the mind; when these stand and are set in the self, in the mind, and become serene, then Brahman shines.
Like fire without smoke, with blazing flame, like the shining sun, like lightning in the sky, he sees the self by the self; and everything is seen there, everywhere, by being pervasive.
The great-souled brahmanas who are wise see him, steadfast, greatly wise, intent on the good of all beings.
So practising for a measured time, of strict vows, sitting alone in solitude, he would reach sameness with the imperishable.
Bewilderment, giddiness and whirling, in smelling, hearing and seeing; marvels in taste and touch, cold and heat; the form of wind;
insight and obstacles also, having been gathered by yoga, the knower of truth should disregard and turn away by his own self.
The restrained sage should practise yoga three times a day; on a mountain peak, at a shrine, and at treetops he should join.
Holding in the grasp of the senses, like one with a vessel in a cow-pen, one-pointed, he should think ever, and not let the mind be disturbed by yoga.
By whatever means the unsteady mind can be restrained, he should follow that one joined, and not stray from it.
Empty mountain caves, temples and empty houses he should resort to for dwelling, one-pointed.
He should not strike at another by speech, deed or mind; indifferent, restrained in food, equal in gain and loss.
Whoever praises him and whoever slanders him, he should be equal to both, and not dwell on good or bad.
He should not rejoice in gains nor think of losses, equal to all beings, of like nature to the wind.
Thus for the good man who is the self of all, seeing equally everywhere, in a few months, ever joined, he passes beyond the word-Brahman.
Seeing creatures afflicted by pain, equal toward clod, stone and gold, devoted to this path, he would stop and not be bewildered.
Even a person of low class or a woman desiring dharma, even those two by this path go to the highest goal.
The unborn, ancient, ageless, eternal, which an unmoving man perceives through the senses, smaller than the small, greater than the great, he sees by the self, self-possessed and joined.
This is the word of the great-souled sage, spoken as it is, observed in the mind; considering it, he reaches sameness with the Supreme, the goal which the wise attain among beings."
[Shuka said:] "I wish to hear this; tell it to me. This, in mutual contradiction, seems to run in opposition."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, the son of Parashara answered his son: "I shall explain these two, action and knowledge, the perishable and the imperishable.
The direction they go by knowledge and that they reach by action: hear, son, one-pointed; this difference is deep.
The one who says "there is dharma" and also that "there is none" here: this would be like that party of mine.
There are these two paths on which the Vedas are established: the dharma marked by activity, and well spoken in withdrawal.
By action the thread is bound; by knowledge it is freed; therefore ascetics who see the far shore do not do action.
By action one is born after death embodied and sixteenfold; by knowledge one is ever born as imperishable, of imperishable nature.
But some men of lesser wisdom praise action; by it they delight in nets of bodies and remain.
Where going one does not die, where going one is not born, where going one does not age or grow;
where is that supreme Brahman, unmanifest, ageless, firm, unobstructed, effortless, immortal and without separation;
where they are not troubled by the pairs, or by mental action, equal everywhere, friendly, and intent on the good of all beings.
One person, dear, is made of knowledge and another of action; know the moon on the new-moon night as standing in a subtle part.
This, said by the sage, is inferred at length: seeing the new moon like a curved thread in the sky.
Eleven-fold in modification, gathered of the stores of parts, know him as embodied, of the nature of action and qualities.
The god who dwells in it like a water drop on a lotus: know him as the knower of the field, ever won over by renunciation.
Know tamas, rajas and sattva as these qualities of the soul; know the soul as the quality of the self, the self of the supreme self.
They say that the soul's quality is consciousness; he moves and moves all; beyond that they call the knower of the field, who sets in motion the seven worlds."
[Shuka said:] "I wish further to hear, in this world, the good conduct and the reasoned conduct by which the good proceed.
In the Veda it is said, "do action" and "give up"; how can I understand this? You should explain it.
Knowing the truth of the world's events, purified by my teacher's command, I shall make up my mind and, with my self released, give up the self without pain."
[Vyasa said:] "This livelihood which was ordained before by Brahma himself has been practised by earlier good great sages.
By celibacy the great sages conquer the worlds; and seek the good of the self in the heart, in the self, by the mind.
In the forest, living on roots and fruit, performing very great austerity, wandering at holy places and harming no beings,
where there is no smoke, the pestle laid down, in a forest-dweller's shelter, going for alms at the proper time, one is fit for Brahman.
Without praise, without salutation, giving up good and bad, wander alone in the forest, eating whatever comes."
[Shuka said:] "I wish to hear this; let the blessed one tell me how it proceeds without contradiction of actions."
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed, the son of Gandhavati answered his son, the sage honouring the words of his son of immeasurable splendour.
Householder, celibate student, forest-dweller and mendicant, all who do as laid down go to the highest goal.
One who rightly follows these stages in turn, free of desire and aversion, is honoured in the next world.
This four-stepped ladder is set in Brahman; relying on this ladder one is honoured in the world of Brahma.
For a quarter of his life the celibate student, free of envy, should dwell with his teacher or his teacher's son, skilled in dharma and wealth.
Wishing to prosper, he should study with the teacher beyond his work, be skilled and not slander; when called, he should attend the teacher.
He should sleep last and rise first in the teacher's house; whatever should be done by a disciple or a servant,
having done it all, saying "it is done," he should stand at the side, a servant doing all, skilled in all tasks.
Pure, skilled, endowed with virtues, he should speak unhurried like an arrow; he should look at the teacher with the eye, unagitated, master of senses.
He should not eat before he has eaten, nor drink before he has drunk, nor sit while he stands, nor sleep while he sleeps.
With palms upturned he should gently touch his feet, the right with the right and the left with the left, pressing.
Having saluted the teacher he should say, "Teach me, blessed one; this I shall do; this I have done."
Having thus got permission for everything and offered wealth to the teacher, he should do it, and having done it all, report again to the teacher.
What perfumes or tastes the celibate student does not use, he may use on returning home: so the determination in dharma.
Whatever rules for celibate students are told in detail, he should observe them all, and not stray from his teacher.
Thus, having brought joy to his teacher as he is able, the disciple should live by action in each stage in turn.
By the Vedic vow and fasting, when the fourth part of his life is gone, having given the fee to the teacher, he should return home by rule.
Joined with a wife obtained by dharma, kindling the fires by dharma, for the second part of his life he should be a householder keeping vows."
[Vyasa said:] "The wise remember four livelihoods of householders: the first with a granary, then with a jar of grain,
then living for one day's need, then that resorting to the pigeon's livelihood. Each later one is better by dharma and wins greater worlds.
One lives on one, another on three, another on two, and the fourth is established in the sacrifice of Brahman. The vows of householders here are called great.
He should not cook food for himself, nor kill animals in vain; a living or lifeless thing is fit for consecration by the Yajus.
He should not sleep by day, nor in the early or late night; he should not eat between times; he should not invite a woman out of season.
No brahmana should stay unhonoured in his house without eating; his guests too are to be honoured, as carriers of offerings to gods and ancestors.

Those bathed in the vow of Vedic learning, learned in the Veda, masters of it, living by their own dharma, self-controlled, active, ascetic: for them the offerings to gods and ancestors are ordained as honour.
Not for one travelling with asses, one ignorant of his own dharma, one who has thrown away the fire-offering, or a teacher who acts like a fool.

He should always be an eater of remains and always eat nectar; nectar is what remains of the sacrifice, food equal to the oblation; one who eats what remains after servants is called an eater of remains.
Devoted to his wife, self-controlled, free of envy, master of his senses, with priests, household priests, teachers, maternal uncles and guests who depend on him,
with the aged, children, sick, physicians, kin, relatives and connections, with mother and father, sisters, brother, son and wife,
with daughter and servants he should not engage in dispute; leaving these quarrels he is freed from all sins.
By conquering these he conquers all worlds, without doubt: the teacher is lord of the world of Brahma, the father lord in the world of Prajapati,
the guest lord of Indra's world, the priests of the world of gods; sisters of the world of apsarases; kin in the Vishvedevas' world;
relations and kinsmen in the directions; mother and maternal uncle on earth; the aged, children, sick and weak in space, powerful.
The elder brother is like a father, the wife and son one's own body, the servants one's shadow, the daughter most pitiable.
Therefore, though insulted by these, he should always bear it, unfevered, devoted to household dharma, learned, constant in dharma, conquering fatigue.
Not bound by wealth, he should practise no action or dharma at all; of the three householder livelihoods, the highest good is in these.
They say of each other that it is the fourfold order of stages; of the rules named for them, all are to be done by one who wishes to prosper.
With granary grain, gleaners and those who have taken the pigeon's livelihood: the realm where these worthy ones dwell prospers.
He purifies ten ancestors before and ten after, and grandfathers, who follows these householder livelihoods without distress.
He would reach a goal like that of the worlds of the wheel-roamers; or this goal is ordained for those of controlled senses.
Heaven is for householders of noble mind, beneficial; heaven joined with aerial cars, flowering, seen in the Veda.
In the world of heaven is the standing of householders of controlled self; this ladder was ordained by Brahma, from which one is freed; reaching the second step in order, he is honoured in heaven.
Beyond this, they call the supreme, noble third stage that of those who give up the body, the forest-dwellers, the unsurpassed of householders; hear this about those who afflict the body."
[Vyasa said:] "Having gradually shaken off this, he takes the third, best livelihood, for forest-dwellers weary of the vow of union.
Hear it, Partha, good luck to you, for those whose selves are the resort of all worlds, who act after reflection, dwelling in holy places.
When the householder sees wrinkles and grey hair on himself and the child of his child, then he should resort to the forest.
He should dwell in the forest-dweller's stage for the third part of his life, tending the same fires, sacrificing to the dwellers of heaven.
Restrained, with restrained diet, eating grain, heedful, he should keep the fire-offering, the cows and all the limbs of sacrifice.
Unploughed rice and barley, wild grain and leavings, he should offer as oblations in the five sacrifices.
In the forest-dweller's stage too four livelihoods are remembered: some wash off at once; some store for a month.
Some store for a year, some for twelve years, for honouring guests and for accomplishing the sacrificial system.
They roll on the ground, or stand on their toes, live by standing and sitting, and bathe at the pressings.
Some use their teeth as mortars, others pound with stones; some drink boiled gruel once in the bright fortnight,
some in the dark fortnight, and eat in order; some on roots, some on fruits, some on flowers, firm in vows,
living properly, relying on the doctrine of the Vaikhanasas; these and many other initiations are theirs, the wise.
The fourth, the dharma of the Upanishads, is held to be common; from the forest-dweller and the householder another proceeds.
In this very age, dear, by brahmanas who see all ends: Agastya, the seven sages, Madhuchchhanda, Aghamarshana,
Sankriti, Sudiva, Tandi, Yavanna, Kritashrama, Ahovirya, Kavya, Tandya, the wise Medhatithi,
Shloka, Nirvaka, Shunyapala, Kritashrama: thus learned in these dharmas, they reached heaven.
Dear, the companies of wandering ascetics, seers of fierce austerity, who saw skill in dharma, with dharma visible,
inexpressible and immeasurable, brahmanas resorted to the forest: Vaikhanasas, Valakhilyas, Sikatas and others.
Joyless in actions, constant in dharma, master of senses, all those with dharma visible resorted to the forest; unmarked and unassailable, they are seen as hosts of lights.
When troubled by age and afflicted by disease, in the fourth part of life that remains he should leave the forest-dweller's stage, having performed the same-day sacrifice with all Vedic fees.
Sacrificing to the self, delighting in the self, with the self for resort, placing the fires in the self, giving up all possessions,
he should perform the same-day sacrifices and the offerings here always; for those who ever sacrifice, he turns from sacrifice to sacrificing in the self.
He should rightly sacrifice the three fires in the self itself, by freeing the self; he should offer the five breaths with the Yajus, eating without blame.
Having shed hair, down and nails, the forest-dweller becomes a sage; from stage to stage, purified by deeds, he goes at once.
The twice-born who goes forth giving fearlessness to all beings has radiant worlds, and after death gains the endless.
Of good conduct, with sin removed, not striving here or in the next world, free of anger and delusion, beyond peace and war, the knower of the self would be as one indifferent.

He should not be pained at the restraints gone into the self, with his own scripture, sutra, oblation, mantra and valour; the self-sacrificer's goal would be as he wishes; there is no doubt for the devoted to dharma, master of senses.
Beyond this, hear of the fourth, supreme stage, the best, exalted by great virtues, above the three, the highest, as it is being described, the supreme refuge."
[Vyasa said:] "Having received refinement from these two stages, what is to be done afterward for the highest aim, hear here one-pointed.
Having ripened the astringency, in three steps of the ladder, one should go forth to the supreme place, the highest wandering mendicancy.
You should live practising so, and hear: one should wander alone ever, for success, without companion.
He who wanders alone, seeing, neither gives up nor is given up; without fire, without home, he should resort to a village for food.
He should be a sage of purified feeling, with the rule of not storing for tomorrow, light of diet, restrained in food, eating once.
The bowl, tree roots, rags, solitude and indifference toward all beings: this much is the mark of a mendicant.
In whom words enter like stones fallen in a well and do not return to the speaker: he should dwell in the stage of isolation.
He should not see or hear what is not to be said about anyone, especially about brahmanas, nor ever speak it.
Covered by whatever, fed by whatever, sleeping wherever: the gods know such a one as of ripened mind.
Afraid of company as of a snake, of luxury as of hell, of women as of a corpse: the gods know him as a brahmana.
He who is neither angry nor glad, honoured or dishonoured, giver of fearlessness to all beings: the gods know him as a brahmana.
He should neither welcome death nor life; he should wait for time alone, like a servant for orders.
His mind should be unstruck and his speech unstruck; freed from all sins, what fear has he with no enemy?
He from whom beings have no fear and through whom they have none, freed from the body, has no fear from any quarter.
As the footprints of other walkers are all covered in the elephant's footprint, so, in non-violence, all footprints of dharma and wealth are covered.
He who adopts non-violence ever dwells as immortal.
The non-violent, equal, truthful, steady, with restrained senses, a refuge of all beings, gains the unsurpassed goal.
Thus for the wise one satisfied with wisdom, fearless, there is no state beyond death; he goes beyond death.
Freed from all attachments, a sage standing like space, without possessions, wandering alone, calm: the gods know him as a brahmana.
He whose life is for dharma, whose dharma is for wealth, and whose days and nights are for merit: the gods know him as a brahmana.
Without hope, without undertaking, without salutation or praise, with deeds spent and unspent: the gods know him as a brahmana.
All beings delight in happiness; all are greatly afraid of pain; so, having been distressed at causing them fear, one with faith would not do actions.
The gift of fearlessness is the fee: all gifts rest on it here; he who first gives up the sharp body gains the endless fearlessness from creatures.
He who offers oblation into the upturned mouth, the navel of the world, the support of the universe: his limbs, what is done and undone, Vaishvanara has entered all.
In the heart, a span in size, that which is lodged: in it the self-sacrificer offers the breaths; his fire-offering, offered and set in the self, is in all those worlds always.
Those who know the divine threefold winged one, the foremost and the supreme truth, honoured in all worlds, become gods, able, and go to merit.
The Vedas and the knowable, the whole rule, and the etymology and the supreme truth: him who knows all in the body-self the gods always desire.
Unattached on earth, immeasurable in heaven, golden, born of the egg, the winged bird in the sky in the middle of the egg: he who knows it, shining with rays in the enjoyable self.
The turning, ageless, revolving, twelve-spoked, well-jointed felly: into whose mouth the universe goes; that wheel of Time is set in the cave.
He who is the grace of the world and its body gains all worlds here; what is offered in him satisfies the gods here, and they, satisfied, satisfy his mouth.
Made of energy, with an eternal body, ancient, he goes to endless fearless worlds; from whom beings are never afraid, he is never afraid of beings.
Not to be blamed, and not blaming others, that brahmana should see the Supreme Self, with delusion removed, sin removed, and gaining nothing here or hereafter.
Free of anger and delusion, equal toward clod and gold, grief gone, peace and war gone, free of blame and praise, of the pleasant and unpleasant, roaming as one indifferent: this is the mendicant."
[Vyasa said:] "With these senses stationed in the mind he does his work here, like a charioteer with well-trained, firm best horses.
Beyond the senses are the objects; beyond the objects, the mind; beyond the mind, intellect; beyond intellect, the great self.
Beyond the great is the unmanifest; beyond the unmanifest, the immortal; beyond the immortal there is nothing; that is the limit, that is the highest goal.
So the self hidden in all beings does not shine; it is seen by the supreme, subtle intellect of those who see the truth.
With the senses, their objects and the many things to be thought merged in the inner self through understanding, thinking nothing,
having ceased from meditation, the mind accomplished by knowledge, without a master, calm of self, he then reaches the immortal state.
Subject to all the senses, with memory unsteady, a mortal meets death by giving himself away.
Having given up all intentions, he should settle the mind in sattva; having settled the mind in sattva, he would be beyond time.
The secret of all the Vedas, without tradition, without scripture, a treatise convincing to the self, this is the teaching to a son.
Among all accounts of dharma and accounts of truth, the wealth is this: ten thousand verses churned, the nectar drawn out.
As butter from curds and fire from wood, so the knowledge of the wise is drawn out for the sake of a son; this teaching is for graduates, to be told to a son.
It should not be told to the unquiet, the not self-controlled, the one without austerity, the one ignorant of the Veda, nor to one who does not follow.
Not to the envious, the crooked, one who does not do as told, one scorched by the science of reasoning, nor to a backbiter.
It is to be told to a praiseworthy, calm ascetic, to a dear son and a following disciple; the secret dharma is not to be told to anyone else in any way.
Even if a man were to give him this whole earth full of jewels, the knower of truth would think this alone the better."
Agni himself loved that royal daughter Sudarshana, and, becoming a brahmana in person, asked that king for her.
His son was Avikshit, a knower of dharma like Yayati, subduer of foes, who brought the earth under his sway; by valour and virtue that king was like a father.
All this is yours; I appease you with my head bowed; we are in your power, king of kings; let the fever of your mind go.
As he struck, the mighty Babhru, conqueror of enemy cities, and Daruka said to the Dasharha what follows; learn it.
Whether good or sin, whatever is the place of my brothers today, that alone I wish to reach; I desire no other worlds.
See him, lord, the tiger among men, the son of the Sun, standing in his own place; mighty-armed bull among men, cast off your grief.
